system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker ~MUT_TP53 (TP53 wild-type (no damaging TP53 mutation)).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

name: scan_target

content.thinking: The MDM2 selectivity looks strong for TP53-wild-type lines, with 196 of 241 strongly dependent versus 124 of 385 in the comparison group. That comparison group is TP53-mutant, so the contrast is really about the TP53 pathway itself. The mechanism is well established, since MDM2 negatively regulates p53 and MDM2 inhibitors like nutlin are known, so this isn't a novel finding. I'll register it and replicate it.

input.mechanism: In TP53 wild-type cells MDM2 continuously ubiquitinates and degrades p53. Knocking out MDM2 releases p53, which activates CDKN1A/BAX/MDM2 feedback and causes growth arrest or apoptosis. TP53-mutant cells lack this axis, so MDM2 is dispensable there. The selective dependency is therefore a direct consequence of wild-type p53 signalling.

steps: Register H1: TP53-WT lines depend on MDM2 (done)
Replicate H1 in held-out Broad and Sanger screens
Submit findings with MDM2 first; note PPM1D/MDM4 as secondary candidates

findings.claim: In TP53 wild-type cancer lines (no damaging TP53 mutation), knockout of MDM2 is selectively lethal relative to TP53-mutant lines (discovery beta -0.84, t=-19.6; held-out Broad p=6e-41; independent Sanger p=8e-17). MDM2 is the top TP53-WT-selective dependency, consistent with its role as the p53 negative regulator.

input.summary: Best candidate for TP53 wild-type cancers is MDM2. It was the top lineage-adjusted selective dependency among the 241 TP53 wild-type discovery lines (mean effect -1.37 vs -0.45 in TP53-mutant lines; 81% of altered lines strongly dependent). It replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=6e-41) and in independent Sanger screens (p=8e-17). The mechanism is the well-known MDM2-p53 axis, so this is not a novel finding, but it validates the data. Secondary candidates from the scan, not tested: PPM1D (beta -0.36, 39% dependent), MDM4 (beta -0.32), and USP7 (broadly essential, so a weaker therapeutic window). MDM2 is also broadly essential, but the TP53-mutant lines show much weaker dependence, which leaves a usable window. Note that the signal reflects p53 pathway status, so it should only be used in TP53 wild-type populations.
